claim: Undifferentiated human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) contain only six TAFs (TAFs 2, 3, 5, 6, 7 and 11).
source: Here we find, unexpectedly, that undifferentiated human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) contain only six TAFs (TAFs 2, 3, 5, 6, 7 and 11), whereas following differentiation all TAFs are expressed.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis (Figure 1A), qRT-PCR (Figure 1B), and ChIP experiments showing only these six TAFs are detectably expressed in H9 cells.

claim: Following differentiation of hESCs, all TAFs are expressed.
source: Here we find, unexpectedly, that undifferentiated human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) contain only six TAFs (TAFs 2, 3, 5, 6, 7 and 11), whereas following differentiation all TAFs are expressed.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis showing TAFs 1, 4, 8, 9, 10, 12, and 13 are induced following retinoic acid treatment (Figure 1D).

claim: Most active genes in hESCs are bound by only TAFs 3 and 5 along with TBP.
source: Directed and global chromatin immunoprecipitation analyses reveal an unprecedented promoter occupancy pattern: most active genes are bound by only TAFs 3 and 5 along with TBP, whereas the remaining active genes are bound by TBP and all six hESC TAFs.
evidence: Supported by ChIP experiments (Figure 3B) and ChIP-chip analyses (Figure 6A) showing class I genes are bound by TAFs 3 and 5.

claim: The remaining active genes in hESCs are bound by TBP and all six hESC TAFs.
source: Directed and global chromatin immunoprecipitation analyses reveal an unprecedented promoter occupancy pattern: most active genes are bound by only TAFs 3 and 5 along with TBP, whereas the remaining active genes are bound by TBP and all six hESC TAFs.
evidence: Supported by ChIP experiments (Figure 3B) and ChIP-chip analyses (Figure 6B, 6C) showing class II genes are bound by all six hESC TAFs.

claim: hESCs contain a previously undescribed complex comprising TAFs 2, 6, 7, 11 and TBP.
source: Consistent with these results, hESCs contain a previously undescribed complex comprising TAFs 2, 6, 7, 11 and TBP.
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient sedimentation (Figure 2A) and co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 2B) showing these TAFs co-sediment and co-immunoprecipitate with TBP.

claim: Altering the composition of hESC TAFs by depleting TAFs that are present results in misregulated expression of pluripotency genes and induction of differentiation.
source: Altering the composition of hESC TAFs, either by depleting TAFs that are present or ectopically expressing TAFs that are absent, results in misregulated expression of pluripotency genes and induction of differentiation.
evidence: Supported by RNAi experiments showing knockdown of hESC TAFs induces differentiation (Figure 8A, 8B) and decreases pluripotency gene expression (Figure 8C).

claim: Altering the composition of hESC TAFs by ectopically expressing TAFs that are absent results in misregulated expression of pluripotency genes and induction of differentiation.
source: Altering the composition of hESC TAFs, either by depleting TAFs that are present or ectopically expressing TAFs that are absent, results in misregulated expression of pluripotency genes and induction of differentiation.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing ectopic expression of TAF1 induces differentiation (Figure 8E, 8F) and decreases pluripotency gene expression (Figure 8F, 8H).

claim: The selective expression and use of TAFs underlies the ability of hESCs to self-renew.
source: Thus, the selective expression and use of TAFs underlies the ability of hESCs to self-renew.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that altering TAF composition results in loss of pluripotency and differentiation.

claim: The general transcription factor TFIID comprises the TATA-box-binding protein (TBP) and approximately 14 TBP-associated factors (TAFs).
source: The general transcription factor TFIID comprises the TATA-box-binding protein (TBP) and approximately 14 TBP-associated factors (TAFs).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about TFIID composition.

claim: General transcription factors are necessary and can be sufficient for accurate transcription initiation in vitro.
source: First, general (or basic) transcription factors (GTFs) are necessary and can be sufficient for accurate transcription initiation in vitro (for review, see Thomas and Chiang, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review article (Thomas and Chiang, 2006).

claim: The basic transcription factors include RNA polymerase II itself and at least six GTFs: TFIID, TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIE, TFIIF and TFIIH.
source: These basic factors include RNA polymerase II itself and at least six GTFs: TFIID, TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIE, TFIIF and TFIIH.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the composition of basic transcription machinery.

claim: The GTFs assemble on the core promoter in an ordered fashion to form a pre-initiation complex (PIC).
source: The GTFs assemble on the core promoter in an ordered fashion to form a pre-initiation complex (PIC).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about transcription initiation.

claim: Activators are sequence-specific DNA-binding proteins whose recognition sites are typically present upstream of the core promoter.
source: In general, activators are sequence-specific DNA-binding proteins whose recognition sites are typically present upstream of the core promoter.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about transcriptional activators.

claim: Activators work in large part by increasing PIC formation.
source: Activators work in large part by increasing PIC formation but can also act through other mechanisms, such as accelerating the rate of transcriptional elongation, promoting multiple rounds of transcription and directing chromatin modifications (reviewed in Green, 2005; Fuda et al., 2009; Weake and Workman, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles (Green, 2005; Fuda et al., 2009; Weake and Workman, 2010).

claim: Activators can act through mechanisms such as accelerating the rate of transcriptional elongation, promoting multiple rounds of transcription and directing chromatin modifications.
source: Activators work in large part by increasing PIC formation but can also act through other mechanisms, such as accelerating the rate of transcriptional elongation, promoting multiple rounds of transcription and directing chromatin modifications (reviewed in Green, 2005; Fuda et al., 2009; Weake and Workman, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles (Green, 2005; Fuda et al., 2009; Weake and Workman, 2010).

claim: The differential expression and use of basic transcription factors can contribute to eukaryotic gene regulation.
source: However, it is now clear that the differential expression and use of basic transcription factors can also contribute to eukaryotic gene regulation (reviewed in Davidson, 2003; Hochheimer and Tjian, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles (Davidson, 2003; Hochheimer and Tjian, 2003).

claim: Studies in yeast demonstrated distinct classes of protein-coding genes that differ by their dependence on and recruitment of TAFs.
source: One of the earliest clues about the differential function of TFIID came from studies in yeast demonstrating distinct classes of protein-coding genes that differ by their dependence on and recruitment of TAFs (Kuras et al., 2000; Li et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies (Kuras et al., 2000; Li et al., 2000).

claim: Similar classes of TAF-dependent and -independent genes were identified in mammalian cells.
source: Subsequently, similar classes of TAF-dependent and -independent genes were identified in mammalian cells (Raha et al., 2005; Tokusumi et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies (Raha et al., 2005; Tokusumi et al., 2007).

claim: TAFs are depleted upon terminal differentiation of muscle.
source: Consistent with the existence of TAF-independent promoters, more recent studies have found that TAFs are depleted upon terminal differentiation of muscle (Deato and Tjian, 2007; Deato et al., 2008) and liver (D'Alessio et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies (Deato and Tjian, 2007; Deato et al., 2008).

claim: TAFs are depleted upon terminal differentiation of liver.
source: Consistent with the existence of TAF-independent promoters, more recent studies have found that TAFs are depleted upon terminal differentiation of muscle (Deato and Tjian, 2007; Deato et al., 2008) and liver (D'Alessio et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study (D'Alessio et al., 2011).

claim: TFIID diversity is promoted by tissue-specific variants of TAFs.
source: TFIID diversity is also promoted by tissue-specific variants of TAFs as well as TBP derivatives referred to as TBP-related factors (reviewed in D'Alessio et al., 2009; Müller et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles (D'Alessio et al., 2009; Müller et al., 2010).

claim: TFIID diversity is promoted by TBP derivatives referred to as TBP-related factors.
source: TFIID diversity is also promoted by tissue-specific variants of TAFs as well as TBP derivatives referred to as TBP-related factors (reviewed in D'Alessio et al., 2009; Müller et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles (D'Alessio et al., 2009; Müller et al., 2010).

claim: Pluripotency and the ability to undergo symmetrical self-renewing divisions in hESCs are largely controlled at the transcriptional level.
source: Two characteristic properties of hESCs, pluripotency, a capacity to differentiate into all fetal and adult cell lineages, and the ability to undergo symmetrical self-renewing divisions, are largely controlled at the transcriptional level (reviewed in Chen and Daley, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review article (Chen and Daley, 2008).

claim: In undifferentiated hESCs, pluripotency genes such as OCT4, NANOG and SOX2 are expressed.
source: In undifferentiated hESCs, pluripotency genes such as OCT4 (also called POU5F1), NANOG and SOX2 are expressed, whereas genes involved in differentiation are transcriptionally inactive (reviewed in Sun et al., 2006; Pan and Thomson, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles (Sun et al., 2006; Pan and Thomson, 2007).

claim: In undifferentiated hESCs, genes involved in differentiation are transcriptionally inactive.
source: In undifferentiated hESCs, pluripotency genes such as OCT4 (also called POU5F1), NANOG and SOX2 are expressed, whereas genes involved in differentiation are transcriptionally inactive (reviewed in Sun et al., 2006; Pan and Thomson, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles (Sun et al., 2006; Pan and Thomson, 2007).

claim: Decreased expression of pluripotency genes induces differentiation.
source: Decreased expression of pluripotency genes induces differentiation (Niwa et al., 2000), and thus proper transcriptional regulation is essential for self-renewal of undifferentiated hESCs.
evidence: Supported by citation to a study (Niwa et al., 2000).

claim: Proper transcriptional regulation is essential for self-renewal of undifferentiated hESCs.
source: Decreased expression of pluripotency genes induces differentiation (Niwa et al., 2000), and thus proper transcriptional regulation is essential for self-renewal of undifferentiated hESCs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that decreased pluripotency gene expression induces differentiation.

claim: All 13 TAFs analyzed were expressed in HeLa cells.
source: The immunoblot of Figure 1A shows, as expected, that all 13 TAFs were expressed in HeLa cells.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: hESCs clearly expressed TAFs 2, 3, 5, 6, 7 and 11.
source: By contrast, hESCs clearly expressed TAFs 2, 3, 5, 6, 7 and 11, whereas expression of TAFs 1, 4, 8, 9, 10, 12, and 13 was undetectable.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Expression of TAFs 1, 4, 8, 9, 10, 12, and 13 was undetectable in hESCs.
source: By contrast, hESCs clearly expressed TAFs 2, 3, 5, 6, 7 and 11, whereas expression of TAFs 1, 4, 8, 9, 10, 12, and 13 was undetectable.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: TAF6 is expressed in both HeLa and H9 cells, but the isoform present in H9 cells is predominantly the short delta form, whereas in HeLa cells, the major TAF6 isoform is the larger, alpha/beta form.
source: Interestingly, TAF6 is expressed in both cell types, but the isoform present in H9 cells is predominantly the short delta form, whereas in HeLa cells, the major TAF6 isoform is the larger, alpha/beta form.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A similar TAF expression pattern was observed in H1 hESC line as in H9 cells.
source: We observed a similar TAF expression pattern in a second hESC line, H1 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: qRT-PCR analysis comparing TAF mRNA levels in HeLa and H9 cells correlated with the immunoblotting results.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR (qRT-PCR) analysis comparing TAF mRNA levels in HeLa and H9 cells correlated with the immunoblotting results (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All other GTFs analyzed were comparably expressed in HeLa and H9 cells.
source: Unlike the TAFs, all other GTFs analyzed were comparably expressed in HeLa and H9 cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Following retinoic acid treatment of H9 cells, expression of the pluripotency factor OCT4 was lost.
source: Figure 1D shows, as expected, that following retinoic acid treatment, expression of the pluripotency factor OCT4 was lost and NES, a neuroectoderm marker, was induced.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Following retinoic acid treatment of H9 cells, NES, a neuroectoderm marker, was induced.
source: Figure 1D shows, as expected, that following retinoic acid treatment, expression of the pluripotency factor OCT4 was lost and NES, a neuroectoderm marker, was induced.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: TAFs 1, 4, 8, 9, 10, 12, and 13, which are not expressed in undifferentiated H9 cells, were induced following retinoic acid treatment.
source: Significantly, TAFs 1, 4, 8, 9, 10, 12, and 13, which are not expressed in undifferentiated H9 cells, were induced following retinoic acid treatment.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: TAFs 2, 3, 5, 6, 7 and 11, which are expressed in undifferentiated H9 cells, were also present at a relatively constant level following retinoic acid treatment.
source: TAFs 2, 3, 5, 6, 7 and 11, which are expressed in undifferentiated H9 cells, were also present at a relatively constant level following retinoic acid treatment.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: TAFs 2, 6, 7 and 11 co-sedimented with an apparent native molecular mass of ∼440 kDa in H9 cell nuclear extract.
source: The results of Figure 2A show that TAFs 2, 6, 7 and 11 co-sedimented with an apparent native molecular mass of ∼440 kDa.
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient sedimentation analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TAFs 3 and 5 fractionated heterogeneously in H9 cell nuclear extract.
source: By contrast, TAFs 3 and 5 fractionated heterogeneously, and a substantial portion of both TAFs had an apparent molecular mass consistent with that of the free proteins (∼140 and ∼100 kDa, respectively).
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient sedimentation analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A substantial portion of TAFs 3 and 5 had an apparent molecular mass consistent with that of the free proteins (∼140 and ∼100 kDa, respectively).
source: By contrast, TAFs 3 and 5 fractionated heterogeneously, and a substantial portion of both TAFs had an apparent molecular mass consistent with that of the free proteins (∼140 and ∼100 kDa, respectively).
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient sedimentation analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TBP fractionated heterogeneously in H9 cell nuclear extract.
source: As expected, TBP, which is associated with multiple complexes involved in transcription by all three RNA polymerases, fractionated heterogeneously.
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient sedimentation analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A peak of TBP co-sedimented with TAFs 2, 6, 7 and 11 in H9 cell nuclear extract.
source: Notably, however, a peak of TBP co-sedimented with TAFs 2, 6, 7 and 11.
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient sedimentation analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TBP was stably associated with TAFs 2, 6, 7 and 11 but not TAFs 3 and 5 in H9 cells.
source: The results of Figure 2B show that TBP was stably associated with TAFs 2, 6, 7 and 11 but not TAFs 3 and 5.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: H9 cells contain a non-canonical TAF complex composed of TBP and TAFs 2, 6, 7 and 11 but not TAFs 3 and 5.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that H9 cells contain a non-canonical TAF complex composed of TBP and TAFs 2, 6, 7 and 11 but not TAFs 3 and 5.
evidence: Inferred from sucrose gradient sedimentation and co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: TBP and POL2 were present at comparable levels at each of 10 active promoters analyzed in H9 cells.
source: As expected, we found that TBP and POL2 were present at comparable levels at each of the 10 promoters (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The absolute level of TBP and POL2 bound to each promoter significantly varied among the 10 genes analyzed.
source: However, the absolute level of TBP and POL2 bound to each promoter significantly varied among the 10 genes.
evidence: Supported by ChIP analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Class I genes were bound by TAFs 3 and 5 but not by TAFs 2, 6, 7 and 11.
source: The first group, which we refer to as class I genes, were bound by TAFs 3 and 5 but not by TAFs 2, 6, 7 and 11, whereas the second group, class II genes, were bound by all six hESC TAFs.
evidence: Supported by ChIP analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Class II genes were bound by all six hESC TAFs.
source: The first group, which we refer to as class I genes, were bound by TAFs 3 and 5 but not by TAFs 2, 6, 7 and 11, whereas the second group, class II genes, were bound by all six hESC TAFs.
evidence: Supported by ChIP analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: TAFs 1, 8 and 9 were readily detected on the promoters of genes in HeLa cells but not H9 cells.
source: The ChIP analysis of Figure 4B shows that TAFs 1, 8 and 9 were readily detected on the promoters of genes in HeLa cells but, as expected, not H9 cells.
evidence: Supported by ChIP analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In both HeLa and H9 cells, TAFs 3 and 5 were recruited to the promoters of seven class I genes.
source: Figure 4C shows that in both cell types TAFs 3 and 5 were recruited to the promoters of the seven genes.
evidence: Supported by ChIP analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: TAFs 2, 6, 7 and 11 were bound to the promoters of seven class I genes in HeLa but not in H9 cells.
source: By contrast we found that TAFs 2, 6, 7 and 11 were bound to the promoters of the seven genes in HeLa but not in H9 cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: On the same transcriptionally active gene the TAF composition is strikingly different in HeLa and H9 cells.
source: These results indicate that on the same transcriptionally active gene the TAF composition is strikingly different in HeLa and H9 cells.
evidence: Inferred from ChIP analysis showing different TAF occupancy patterns on the same genes in HeLa vs H9 cells.

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of TAFs 3 and 5 in H9 cells greatly reduced expression of both class I and II genes.
source: The qRT-PCR results of Figure 5A show that siRNA-mediated knockdown of TAFs 3 and 5 in H9 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) greatly reduced expression of both class I and II genes.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of TAFs 2, 6, 7 and 11 decreased expression of class II genes but did not affect expression of class I genes.
source: By contrast, siRNA-mediated knockdown of TAFs 2, 6, 7 and 11 decreased expression of class II, but did not affect expression of class I genes (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There is a strong relationship between TAF occupancy and transcriptional activity in hESCs.
source: Collectively, these results establish a strong relationship between TAF occupancy and transcriptional activity in hESCs.
evidence: Inferred from RNAi experiments showing that knockdown of TAFs affects expression of genes they occupy.

claim: Approximately 3600 high-confidence actively transcribed genes were defined based upon co-occupancy of both TBP and POL2 at the transcription start-site.
source: We first defined a group of ∼3600 high-confidence actively transcribed genes based upon co-occupancy of both TBP and POL2 at the transcription start-site (Figure 6—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-chip analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: The vast majority of active genes had promoter-bound TAF3 and TAF5.
source: The vast majority of active genes had promoter-bound TAF3 and TAF5 (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-chip analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A smaller fraction of active genes had promoter-bound TAF7 or TAF11.
source: Significantly, a smaller fraction of active genes had promoter-bound TAF7 or TAF11, and there was substantial overlap between TAF7- and TAF11-bound genes (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-chip analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There was substantial overlap between TAF7- and TAF11-bound genes.
source: Significantly, a smaller fraction of active genes had promoter-bound TAF7 or TAF11, and there was substantial overlap between TAF7- and TAF11-bound genes (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-chip analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The vast majority of genes bound by TAFs 7 and 11 were also bound by TAFs 3 and 5.
source: As expected, the vast majority of genes bound by TAFs 7 and 11 were also bound by TAFs 3 and 5 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-chip analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The promoters of class I genes had greater histone H3 lysine 4 trimethylation (H3K4me3) than those of class II genes.
source: First, the promoters of class I genes had greater histone H3 lysine 4 trimethylation (H3K4me3) than those of class II genes (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-chip analysis shown in Figure 6E and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: The fraction of genes with alternative promoters was significantly higher for class II than for class I genes.
source: Second, the fraction of genes with alternative promoters (identified based upon UCSC Genome Browser annotations; see 'Materials and methods') was significantly higher for class II than for class I genes (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-chip analysis shown in Figure 6F and statistical analysis in Table 1.

claim: TAF7 occupancy validated at 24 of 27 predicted sites (88.9%).
source: Most importantly, Figure 7B shows that TAF7 occupancy validated at 24 of 27 predicted sites (88.9%), TAF11 occupancy at 27 of 28 predicted sites (96.4%), TAF3 occupancy at 36 of 39 predicted sites (92.3%), and TAF5 occupancy at 39 of 39 predicted sites (100.0%).
evidence: Supported by directed ChIP validation experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: TAF11 occupancy validated at 27 of 28 predicted sites (96.4%).
source: Most importantly, Figure 7B shows that TAF7 occupancy validated at 24 of 27 predicted sites (88.9%), TAF11 occupancy at 27 of 28 predicted sites (96.4%), TAF3 occupancy at 36 of 39 predicted sites (92.3%), and TAF5 occupancy at 39 of 39 predicted sites (100.0%).
evidence: Supported by directed ChIP validation experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: TAF3 occupancy validated at 36 of 39 predicted sites (92.3%).
source: Most importantly, Figure 7B shows that TAF7 occupancy validated at 24 of 27 predicted sites (88.9%), TAF11 occupancy at 27 of 28 predicted sites (96.4%), TAF3 occupancy at 36 of 39 predicted sites (92.3%), and TAF5 occupancy at 39 of 39 predicted sites (100.0%).
evidence: Supported by directed ChIP validation experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: TAF5 occupancy validated at 39 of 39 predicted sites (100.0%).
source: Most importantly, Figure 7B shows that TAF7 occupancy validated at 24 of 27 predicted sites (88.9%), TAF11 occupancy at 27 of 28 predicted sites (96.4%), TAF3 occupancy at 36 of 39 predicted sites (92.3%), and TAF5 occupancy at 39 of 39 predicted sites (100.0%).
evidence: Supported by directed ChIP validation experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: TAF7 was present at 7 of 7 predicted TAF11-only sites.
source: Specifically, the results show that TAF7 was present at 7 of 7 predicted TAF11-only sites, and TAF11 was present at 5 of 6 predicted TAF7-only sites, indicating that TAF7 and 11 co-occupancy was 12 of 13 (92.3%).
evidence: Supported by directed ChIP validation experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: TAF11 was present at 5 of 6 predicted TAF7-only sites.
source: Specifically, the results show that TAF7 was present at 7 of 7 predicted TAF11-only sites, and TAF11 was present at 5 of 6 predicted TAF7-only sites, indicating that TAF7 and 11 co-occupancy was 12 of 13 (92.3%).
evidence: Supported by directed ChIP validation experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: TAF7 and 11 co-occupancy was 12 of 13 (92.3%).
source: Specifically, the results show that TAF7 was present at 7 of 7 predicted TAF11-only sites, and TAF11 was present at 5 of 6 predicted TAF7-only sites, indicating that TAF7 and 11 co-occupancy was 12 of 13 (92.3%).
evidence: Inferred from directed ChIP validation experiments.

claim: Of the 16 promoters analyzed that were bound by TAF7 and TAF11, TAF2 was present at 16 and TAF6 was present at 15 of these promoters.
source: For example, of the 16 promoters analyzed that were bound by TAF7 and TAF11, TAF2 was present at 16 and TAF6 was present at 15 of these promoters.
evidence: Supported by ChIP analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of each of the six hESC TAFs induced differentiation, as evidenced by a decreased percentage of alkaline phosphatase-positive colonies.
source: Figure 8A shows that shRNA-mediated knockdown of each of the six hESC TAFs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) induced differentiation, as evidenced by a decreased percentage of alkaline phosphatase-positive colonies.
evidence: Supported by alkaline phosphatase staining shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Depletion of each hESC TAF resulted in up-regulation of differentiation markers AFP, CGB7, IGF2, NES and SOX1.
source: Figure 8B shows that depletion of each hESC TAF resulted in up-regulation, to varying extents, of these differentiation markers.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The induction of differentiation following knockdown of hESC TAFs was evidenced by decreased expression of the pluripotency gene NANOG.
source: Finally, the induction of differentiation following knockdown of hESC TAFs was also evidenced by decreased expression of the pluripotency genes NANOG (Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 4) and OCT4 (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 4.

claim: The induction of differentiation following knockdown of hESC TAFs was evidenced by decreased expression of the pluripotency gene OCT4.
source: Finally, the induction of differentiation following knockdown of hESC TAFs was also evidenced by decreased expression of the pluripotency genes NANOG (Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 4) and OCT4 (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The hESC TAFs are required to maintain the undifferentiated state.
source: Thus, the hESC TAFs are required to maintain the undifferentiated state.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that knockdown of hESC TAFs induces differentiation.

claim: Ectopic expression of TAF1 resulted in differentiation, as evidenced by a decreased number of alkaline phosphatase-positive colonies.
source: We found that ectopic expression of TAF1 (Figure 8D) resulted in differentiation, as evidenced by a decreased number of alkaline phosphatase-positive colonies (Figure 8E), the induction of differentiation markers (Figure 8F, left), and decreased expression of NANOG (Figure 8F, right).
evidence: Supported by alkaline phosphatase staining shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Ectopic expression of TAF1 resulted in the induction of differentiation markers.
source: We found that ectopic expression of TAF1 (Figure 8D) resulted in differentiation, as evidenced by a decreased number of alkaline phosphatase-positive colonies (Figure 8E), the induction of differentiation markers (Figure 8F, left), and decreased expression of NANOG (Figure 8F, right).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Ectopic expression of TAF1 resulted in decreased expression of NANOG.
source: We found that ectopic expression of TAF1 (Figure 8D) resulted in differentiation, as evidenced by a decreased number of alkaline phosphatase-positive colonies (Figure 8E), the induction of differentiation markers (Figure 8F, left), and decreased expression of NANOG (Figure 8F, right).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Ectopic TAF1 expression decreased expression of several class II genes, including OCT4.
source: Interestingly, Figure 8G shows that ectopic TAF1 expression decreased expression of several class II genes, including as expected OCT4, whereas expression of class I genes was either unaffected or in some instances increased modestly.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Ectopic TAF1 expression resulted in expression of class I genes being either unaffected or in some instances increased modestly.
source: Interestingly, Figure 8G shows that ectopic TAF1 expression decreased expression of several class II genes, including as expected OCT4, whereas expression of class I genes was either unaffected or in some instances increased modestly.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Ectopic expression of several other TAFs not present in hESCs resulted in loss of expression of OCT4, a class II gene, but not ACTB, a class I gene.
source: Ectopic expression of several other TAFs not present in hESCs also resulted in loss of expression of OCT4, a class II gene, but not ACTB, a class I gene (Figure 8H).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 8H.

claim: Ectopic expression of TBP or TAFs that are present in hESCs did not affect OCT4 levels.
source: By contrast, ectopic expression of TBP or TAFs that are present in hESCs did not affect OCT4 levels.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 8H.

claim: Following ectopic expression of TAF1, TBP and POL2 were no longer recruited to the OCT4 promoter.
source: Figure 8I shows that, following ectopic expression of TAF1, TBP and POL2 were no longer recruited to the OCT4 promoter.
evidence: Supported by ChIP analysis shown in Figure 8I.

claim: Altering the composition of hESC TAFs results in misregulation of gene expression and induction of differentiation.
source: Collectively, the results of Figure 8 show that altering the composition of hESC TAFs results in misregulation of gene expression and induction of differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that both knockdown and ectopic expression of TAFs induce differentiation.

claim: The composition of hESC TAFs is unprecedented and is likely highly specific, if not unique, to hESCs.
source: Previous studies have reported tissue-specific TAF variants and alterations in TAF expression (reviewed in D'Alessio et al., 2009; Müller et al., 2010), but the composition of hESC TAFs is unprecedented and is likely highly specific, if not unique, to hESCs.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with previous studies and the finding that mouse ESCs express all TAFs.

claim: Mouse ESCs express all TFIID TAFs analyzed.
source: For example, we find that mouse ESCs, which bear both similarities and differences to hESCs (Ginis et al., 2004; Wei et al., 2005; Schnerch et al., 2010), express all TFIID TAFs analyzed (Figure 9), consistent with the results of a recent study that focused on the role of TAF3 in mouse ESCs (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 9 and citation to Liu et al., 2011.

claim: The absence of seven of the conventional TFIID TAFs suggested that hESCs contain an alternative TBP-containing complex.
source: The absence of seven of the conventional TFIID TAFs suggested that hESCs contain an alternative TBP-containing complex.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that only six TAFs are expressed in hESCs.

claim: A stable complex containing TBP and TAFs 2, 6, 7 and 11 is recruited to active class II genes.
source: Our ChIP and biochemical experiments confirmed this possibility and revealed a model in which a stable complex containing TBP and TAFs 2, 6, 7 and 11 is recruited to active class II genes, and TAFs 3 and 5 are recruited independently to all active genes (Figure 8J).
evidence: Inferred from ChIP and biochemical experiments showing this complex exists and is recruited to class II genes.

claim: TAFs 3 and 5 are recruited independently to all active genes.
source: Our ChIP and biochemical experiments confirmed this possibility and revealed a model in which a stable complex containing TBP and TAFs 2, 6, 7 and 11 is recruited to active class II genes, and TAFs 3 and 5 are recruited independently to all active genes (Figure 8J).
evidence: Inferred from ChIP and biochemical experiments showing TAFs 3 and 5 are not part of the TBP/TAF 2,6,7,11 complex but are recruited to all active genes.

claim: The novel TBP-containing complex lacks TAF1, which in the canonical TFIID complex interacts directly with TBP.
source: Notably, this novel TBP-containing complex lacks TAF1, which in the canonical TFIID complex interacts directly with TBP (Chen et al., 1994), and TAF4, which is essential for assembly of Drosophila TFIID (Wright et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies (Chen et al., 1994; Wright et al., 2006).

claim: The novel TBP-containing complex lacks TAF4, which is essential for assembly of Drosophila TFIID.
source: Notably, this novel TBP-containing complex lacks TAF1, which in the canonical TFIID complex interacts directly with TBP (Chen et al., 1994), and TAF4, which is essential for assembly of Drosophila TFIID (Wright et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study (Wright et al., 2006).

claim: Previous studies have described interactions between TBP and TAF2.
source: However, consistent with the existence of a TBP/TAF 2,6,7,11 complex, previous studies have described interactions between TBP and TAF2 (Verrijzer et al., 1994), TAF6 (Weinzierl et al., 1993) and TAF11 (Lavigne et al., 1996), and between TAF7 and TAF11 (Lavigne et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study (Verrijzer et al., 1994).

claim: Previous studies have described interactions between TBP and TAF6.
source: However, consistent with the existence of a TBP/TAF 2,6,7,11 complex, previous studies have described interactions between TBP and TAF2 (Verrijzer et al., 1994), TAF6 (Weinzierl et al., 1993) and TAF11 (Lavigne et al., 1996), and between TAF7 and TAF11 (Lavigne et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study (Weinzierl et al., 1993).

claim: Previous studies have described interactions between TBP and TAF11.
source: However, consistent with the existence of a TBP/TAF 2,6,7,11 complex, previous studies have described interactions between TBP and TAF2 (Verrijzer et al., 1994), TAF6 (Weinzierl et al., 1993) and TAF11 (Lavigne et al., 1996), and between TAF7 and TAF11 (Lavigne et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study (Lavigne et al., 1996).

claim: Previous studies have described interactions between TAF7 and TAF11.
source: However, consistent with the existence of a TBP/TAF 2,6,7,11 complex, previous studies have described interactions between TBP and TAF2 (Verrijzer et al., 1994), TAF6 (Weinzierl et al., 1993) and TAF11 (Lavigne et al., 1996), and between TAF7 and TAF11 (Lavigne et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study (Lavigne et al., 1996).

claim: Nine of the 14 TFIID TAFs contain a sequence motif homologous to histones, called the histone fold domain (HFD), which mediates protein–protein interactions.
source: Previous studies have shown that nine of the 14 TFIID TAFs contain a sequence motif homologous to histones, called the histone fold domain (HFD), which mediates protein–protein interactions (reviewed in Cler et al., 2009; Papai et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles (Cler et al., 2009; Papai et al., 2011).

claim: The nine HFD-containing TAFs can form five specific heterodimers: TAF3–10, TAF6–9, TAF4–12, TAF8–10 and TAF11–13.
source: These nine TAFs can form five specific heterodimers: TAF3–10, TAF6–9, TAF4–12, TAF8–10 and TAF11–13.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about TAF heterodimer formation.

claim: Several TAF heterodimers are thought to be important for the assembly and structure of TFIID.
source: Several of these heterodimers are thought to be important for the assembly and structure of TFIID.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about TFIID assembly.

claim: hESCs contain only three HFD-containing TAFs (3, 6 and 11), which cannot form any of the five known heterodimers.
source: hESCs contain only three HFD-containing TAFs (3, 6 and 11), which cannot form any of the five known heterodimers.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that hESCs express only TAFs 3, 6, and 11 among the HFD-containing TAFs.

claim: There are major differences in assembly and structure of TFIID and the TBP/TAF 2,6,7,11 complex.
source: This observation strongly suggests there are major differences in assembly and structure of TFIID and the TBP/TAF 2,6,7,11 complex.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that hESC TAFs cannot form known heterodimers important for TFIID assembly.

claim: Differential recruitment of TAFs can be due to promoter-bound activators, core promoter elements, or both.
source: Studies in yeast have shown that differential recruitment of TAFs can be due to promoter-bound activators, core promoter elements, or both (Shen and Green, 1997; Li et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies (Shen and Green, 1997; Li et al., 2002).

claim: TAF2 and TAF6 have been shown to interact with promoter sequence elements.
source: In this regard, TAF2 and TAF6 have been shown to interact with promoter sequence elements (reviewed in Maston et al., 2006), which may contribute to differential promoter recognition by the TBP/TAF 2,6,7,11 complex.
evidence: Supported by citation to a review article (Maston et al., 2006).

claim: TAF3 contains a PHD finger domain that can bind to the H3K4me3 chromatin mark.
source: In addition, TAF3 contains a PHD finger domain that can bind to the H3K4me3 chromatin mark (Vermeulen et al., 2007), which is enriched at class I promoters (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study (Vermeulen et al., 2007).

claim: H3K4me3 is enriched at class I promoters.
source: In addition, TAF3 contains a PHD finger domain that can bind to the H3K4me3 chromatin mark (Vermeulen et al., 2007), which is enriched at class I promoters (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-chip analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Gene ontology analysis did not reveal any functional category that was differentially enriched in either class I or class II genes.
source: Gene ontology analysis did not reveal any functional category that was differentially enriched in either class I or class II genes (data not shown).
evidence: Stated as a result of gene ontology analysis performed by the authors.

claim: Several pluripotency factors including OCT4 and NANOG are encoded by class II genes.
source: For example, although several pluripotency factors including OCT4 (Figure 3B) and NANOG (Figure 10) are encoded by class II genes, we found other pluripotency factors, such as SOX2, DPPA4 and KLF4, that are encoded by class I genes (Figure 10).
evidence: Supported by ChIP analysis shown in Figure 3B and Figure 10.

claim: Other pluripotency factors, such as SOX2, DPPA4 and KLF4, are encoded by class I genes.
source: For example, although several pluripotency factors including OCT4 (Figure 3B) and NANOG (Figure 10) are encoded by class II genes, we found other pluripotency factors, such as SOX2, DPPA4 and KLF4, that are encoded by class I genes (Figure 10).
evidence: Supported by ChIP analysis shown in Figure 10.

claim: Alternative promoter use has been suggested to play a role in generating tissue-specific transcripts.
source: Notably, alternative promoter use has been suggested to play a role in generating tissue-specific transcripts (Kimura et al., 2006; Kolle et al., 2011; Pal et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies (Kimura et al., 2006; Kolle et al., 2011; Pal et al., 2011).

claim: Genes that are broadly expressed, such as housekeeping genes, can be activated by diverse core promoter recognition complexes in different cell types.
source: Our ChIP experiments show that genes that are broadly expressed, such as housekeeping genes, can be activated by diverse core promoter recognition complexes in different cell types (Figure 4C), revealing a remarkable plasticity of the transcription machinery.
evidence: Supported by ChIP analysis shown in Figure 4C comparing TAF occupancy in HeLa and H9 cells.

claim: The transcription machinery exhibits remarkable plasticity.
source: Our ChIP experiments show that genes that are broadly expressed, such as housekeeping genes, can be activated by diverse core promoter recognition complexes in different cell types (Figure 4C), revealing a remarkable plasticity of the transcription machinery.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the same genes use different TAF complexes in different cell types.

claim: In the myogenic program, core promoter recognition complex changes correlate with the presence of developmentally regulated activators.
source: For example, in the myogenic program, core promoter recognition complex changes correlates with the presence of developmentally regulated activators (Deato et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study (Deato et al., 2008).

claim: The unusual composition of TAFs in hESCs is required for the ability of hESCs to properly regulate gene expression, maintain an undifferentiated state, and self-renew.
source: Thus, the unusual composition of TAFs described here is required for the ability of hESCs to properly regulate gene expression, maintain an undifferentiated state, and self-renew.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that altering TAF composition results in differentiation.

claim: The TAFs that are absent from undifferentiated hESCs are expressed following differentiation.
source: This conclusion is reinforced by the finding that the TAFs that are absent from undifferentiated hESCs are expressed following differentiation (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The transcriptional induction of several differentiation markers following knockdown of an hESC TAF can be explained either by the dispensability of the TAF for transcription of the marker, or incomplete knockdown enabling transcription to occur at reduced TAF levels.
source: The transcriptional induction of several differentiation markers, which are not normally expressed in hESCs, following knockdown of an hESC TAF can be explained either by the dispensability of the TAF for transcription of the marker, or incomplete knockdown enabling transcription to occur at reduced TAF levels.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms to explain the observed results.

claim: A characteristic feature of the switch of undifferentiated hESCs to the differentiated state is the loss of pluripotency gene expression.
source: A characteristic feature of the switch of undifferentiated hESCs to the differentiated state is the loss of pluripotency gene expression.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about hESC differentiation.

claim: Ectopic expression of TAFs that are not present in undifferentiated hESCs results in transcriptional inactivation of pluripotency genes.
source: We have shown that ectopic expression of TAFs that are not present in undifferentiated hESCs results in transcriptional inactivation of pluripotency genes.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing ectopic TAF expression decreases pluripotency gene expression (Figure 8F, 8G, 8H).

claim: The transcriptional induction of TFIID TAFs that are absent from undifferentiated hESCs may be at least part of the mechanism by which pluripotency genes are silenced following differentiation.
source: Thus, the transcriptional induction of TFIID TAFs that are absent from undifferentiated hESCs may be at least part of the mechanism by which pluripotency genes are silenced following differentiation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that ectopic TAF expression silences pluripotency genes.

claim: Terminal differentiation of muscle is accompanied by loss of TFIID TAFs.
source: As discussed above, previous studies have shown that terminal differentiation of muscle (Deato and Tjian, 2007) and liver (D'Alessio et al., 2011) is accompanied by loss of TFIID TAFs.
evidence: Supported by citation to a study (Deato and Tjian, 2007).

claim: Terminal differentiation of liver is accompanied by loss of TFIID TAFs.
source: As discussed above, previous studies have shown that terminal differentiation of muscle (Deato and Tjian, 2007) and liver (D'Alessio et al., 2011) is accompanied by loss of TFIID TAFs.
evidence: Supported by citation to a study (D'Alessio et al., 2011).

claim: During differentiation the canonical TFIID complex becomes progressively specialized.
source: These and other findings have prompted speculation that during differentiation the canonical TFIID complex becomes progressively specialized (reviewed in D'Alessio et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review article (D'Alessio et al., 2009).

claim: Undifferentiated hESCs start with a specialized, highly unique general transcription machinery, then switch to a period of complete TFIID before specialization of the transcription machinery again in some terminal differentiation programs.
source: Rather than starting from a complete, canonical TFIID and progressing to more restricted forms, undifferentiated hESCs start with a specialized, highly unique general transcription machinery, then switch to a period of complete TFIID before specialization of the transcription machinery again in some terminal differentiation programs.
evidence: Inferred from the findings that hESCs have incomplete TFIID, differentiated cells have complete TFIID, and terminally differentiated cells can have specialized TFIID.

claim: Altering the composition of the basic transcription machinery in general and TAFs specifically may be a particularly powerful mechanism for developmental reprogramming.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that altering the composition of the basic transcription machinery in general and TAFs specifically may be a particularly powerful mechanism for developmental reprogramming.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings about TAF composition changes during development.
